questiontext.text: What data structure is a skip list built from?

answer.text: A multi-level linked list where higher levels skip over many nodes

feedback.text: Correct — express lanes above the base list let searches skip ahead.

answer.text: A bit array indexed by k hash functions

feedback.text: That describes a Bloom filter, not a skip list.

answer.text: A contiguous array kept in sorted order

feedback.text: No — a skip list is pointer-based, not array-based.

answer.text: A height-balanced binary search tree with rotations

feedback.text: No — a skip list is an alternative to balanced BSTs and uses no rotations.

generalfeedback.text: A skip list stacks several linked lists; the bottom holds all elements in order and each higher level is a sparse express lane over the one below.

questiontext.text: How is the number of levels (height) of a newly inserted skip-list node decided?

answer.text: Randomly, e.g. by repeatedly flipping a coin until it comes up tails

feedback.text: Correct — each level is promoted with probability p (often 1/2), giving expected balance.

answer.text: By computing the exact median of the stored keys

feedback.text: No — heights are random, not derived from key values.

answer.text: By hashing the key with k hash functions

feedback.text: No — that is a Bloom filter idea; skip lists use coin flips.

answer.text: By performing tree rotations after each insert

feedback.text: No — skip lists never rotate; heights come from randomization.

generalfeedback.text: Each node's height is chosen by a randomized coin-flip process, so the level structure is probabilistically balanced without any deterministic rebalancing.

questiontext.text: What is the expected time complexity of search, insert, and delete in a skip list?

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: Correct — the express lanes halve the search range on average.
No — you still traverse roughly log n levels on average.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: No — that is too slow; a single operation is expected O(log n).
No — even the worst case for one operation is only O(n).

generalfeedback.text: Because higher levels skip about half the remaining nodes, expected search/insert/delete cost is O(log n).

questiontext.text: Why are skip lists often preferred over balanced binary search trees in practice?

answer.text: They are simpler to implement, needing no rotations or rebalancing logic

feedback.text: Correct — randomization replaces the intricate rebalancing of AVL/red-black trees.

answer.text: They guarantee O(log n) worst case unlike any BST

feedback.text: No — a skip list's worst case is O(n); balanced BSTs give O(log n) worst case.

answer.text: They use O(1) total space regardless of n

feedback.text: No — a skip list uses O(n) space, like a BST.

answer.text: They eliminate false positives

feedback.text: No — false positives are a Bloom-filter concept, unrelated to skip lists.

generalfeedback.text: Skip lists achieve BST-like performance with far simpler code, since coin-flip heights avoid explicit rotations and rebalancing.

questiontext.text: Although expected search time is O(log n), a skip list's worst-case search time is O(n).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — an unlucky sequence of coin flips can leave nearly every node at level 1.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — the O(log n) bound is only expected; the rare worst case degrades to O(n).

questiontext.text: A skip list keeps itself balanced by performing rotations after each insertion, just like an AVL tree.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — skip lists never rotate; they rely on randomized node heights instead.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — balance is probabilistic via coin flips, with no rotations at all.

questiontext.text: Each horizontal express lane in a skip list, stacked above the base list, is called a ______.

answer.text: level

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: level*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: layer

feedback.text: Correct — a level (layer) of the skip list.

questiontext.text: Which statements about skip lists are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: They are a probabilistic, randomized data structure

feedback.text: Yes — node heights come from random coin flips.

answer.text: They keep elements in sorted order and support ordered traversal

feedback.text: Yes — the bottom level is a sorted linked list.

answer.text: They guarantee O(log n) time in the worst case

feedback.text: No — only expected time is O(log n); worst case is O(n).

answer.text: They store no keys and can only test membership

feedback.text: No — that is a Bloom filter; skip lists store keys and support ordered operations.

generalfeedback.text: Skip lists are randomized, ordered structures with expected O(log n) operations and O(n) space; the worst case is O(n), and they do store their keys.
